Create a scalar UDF with {{c1::CREATE FUNCTION}} dbo.CalculateSalesTax(@Amount DECIMAL(10,2), @TaxRate DECIMAL(5,4)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) AS BEGIN RETURN @Amount * @TaxRate; END;
column2:
The two inputs supply the amount and rate. RETURNS fixes the result type, and RETURN supplies the calculated value.
Review source

column1: Declare a tax function's result type with {{c1::RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)}} in its header.
column2:
This clause declares the function's output type, not an input type. The returned calculation must be converted to the declared scale.
Review source

column1: Return a scalar variable's value with {{c1::RETURN @TaxAmount}}; inside the function body.
column2:
RETURN passes the variable's value back to the SQL expression that called the function. It is not a procedure's status code.
Review source

column1: Call dbo.CalculateSalesTax for Amount and TaxRate columns with SELECT {{c1::dbo.CalculateSalesTax(Amount, TaxRate)}} FROM dbo.Orders;
column2:
The call takes values from the order row and produces one result in the SELECT list. In Fabric Warehouse, queries on user tables require an eligible inlined scalar call.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: A parameterless scalar UDF call still needs {{c1::parentheses}}, as in SELECT dbo.GetCode();
column2:
Use an empty argument list even when the function needs no inputs. Unlike a column name, the function reference includes the call syntax.
Review source

column1: The tenure calculation's call to {{c1::GETDATE()}} introduces nondeterminism.
column2:
GETDATE reads the current clock. Two calls with the same hire date can see different dates and return different results.
Review source

column1: To make a date calculation repeatable, pass its {{c1::as-of date}} as an argument instead of reading GETDATE().
column2:
When the caller supplies the date, the result no longer depends on the system clock. Use repeatable operations for the rest of the calculation too.
Review source

column1: Before SQL Server can mark a T-SQL UDF deterministic, the definition must use {{c1::SCHEMABINDING}}.
column2:
Schema binding is required for SQL Server to mark a T-SQL function deterministic. It cannot turn a changing input like GETDATE into a repeatable value.
Review source

column1: SELECT DATEDIFF(YEAR, '20241231', '20250101'); returns {{c1::1}}.
column2:
DATEDIFF counts the midnight boundary between the two calendar years. It does not require twelve months to elapse.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2019 and later, automatic scalar UDF inlining requires database compatibility level {{c1::150 or higher}}.
column2:
Compatibility level 150 makes the feature available in supported engines. A setting, function restriction, or calling-query restriction can still prevent inlining.
Review source

column1: A T-SQL scalar UDF can assign local variables but cannot directly update {{c1::permanent database tables}}.
column2:
Local assignments are part of calculating the return value. The function cannot use them as a way to change rows in application tables.
Review source

column1: Modify the existing definition with {{c1::ALTER FUNCTION}} dbo.CalculateSalesTax(@Amount DECIMAL(10,2), @TaxRate DECIMAL(5,4)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) AS BEGIN RETURN @Amount * @TaxRate; END;
column2:
ALTER FUNCTION keeps the object and its granted permissions. If you change the input or output contract, update any callers that depend on the old form.
Review source

column1: Skip removal of a missing function with DROP FUNCTION {{c1::IF EXISTS}} dbo.CalculateSalesTax;
column2:
IF EXISTS makes it safe to repeat the drop when the function is already absent. Permissions and schema-bound references still apply when it exists.
Review source

column1: Inspect recorded object references in {{c1::sys.sql_expression_dependencies}} before removing a scalar UDF.
column2:
Use the view to find recorded SQL expressions that depend on the function. Inspect application code separately if clients can call it directly.
Review source

column1: The formatted phone value '(123) 456-7890' needs {{c1::14}} ASCII characters of return capacity.
column2:
The four formatting characters are two parentheses, a space, and a hyphen. The output type must fit those characters as well as all ten digits.
Review source

column1: To use a scalar UDF parameter's default in a SELECT expression, pass {{c1::DEFAULT}} in that argument position.
column2:
In an expression call, DEFAULT explicitly asks for the parameter's declared value. Leaving the argument position out is not equivalent to a procedure call that omits an optional argument.
Review source
